body:
tl;dr the router-outlet reactivates itself when recreating an element, even when it's not supposed to

Performed some tests and found out some more information.
It seems that the old router-outlet gets reactivated when recreating the element. By manually deactivating the router-outlet, if it's not expected, in the ngAfterViewInit call, I can bypass the issue.

The reason routing broke is that the primary router outlet is active, but it's not supposed to be. When trying to navigate the router then tries to activate the router-outlet (as in its internal state, it's not activated yet). However, the router-outlet is already activated.
Normally this would throw an error, but somehow this error isn't thrown either.

body:
> tl;dr the router-outlet reactivates itself when recreating an element, even when it's not supposed to
> 
> Performed some tests and found out some more information. It seems that the old router-outlet gets reactivated when recreating the element. By manually deactivating the router-outlet, if it's not expected, in the ngAfterViewInit call, I can bypass the issue.
> 
> The reason routing broke is that the primary router outlet is active, but it's not supposed to be. When trying to navigate the router then tries to activate the router-outlet (as in its internal state, it's not activated yet). However, the router-outlet is already activated. Normally this would throw an error, but somehow this error isn't thrown either.

I am trying to implement your bypass but I am struggling to figure out how you did it. Can perhaps give an example that myself and others running into this issue can use?

The issue here (after updating the example to v14) is that the new `RouterOutlet` instance is getting created and initialized before the `ngOnDestroy` runs for the one being removed. If I put the creation and insertion of the new element inside a `setTimeout(() => {...}, 10)` to ensure correct ordering, then the issue is resolved. 

If the `ngOnDestroy` were to pass the outlet instance here https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/0934011b03aae6a4848ab4eeacc896061f4dceca/packages/router/src/directives/router_outlet.ts#L186 and the context did not clear the outlet if the instance is already set to a different one
https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/0934011b03aae6a4848ab4eeacc896061f4dceca/packages/router/src/router_outlet_context.ts#L55-L59
then I believe that would resolve the issue in Angular as well. While this seems to make sense, I'm a bit hesitant to implement this fix without more of a signal that it should be done and is correct.

As a workaround, you can either use the `setTimeout` trick or implement your own `RouterOutlet` by copy-pasting the existing one and doing the same type of logic in the `ngOnDestroy` (call `getContext` and only then call `onChildOutletDestroyed` if the returned context instance is the same as `this`).

Looks like the same timing issue is happening in https://github.com/angular/angular/issues/32453. Since this isn't an isolated use-case anymore and the layout of the application described there is normal, I'll address this directly in the `RouterOutlet`. The issue there is that the constructor where the outlet gets registered is called before the lifecycle hooks `ngOnDestroy` and `ngOnInit` so even though the `ngOnDestroy` of the old one is called first, the new one is already registered.
